deep_why: MetriKG computes measurements of how knowledge graphs evolve—structural features like connectivity, cohesion, and depth. The method works because a knowledge graph is fundamentally a set of relationships between entities, and counting or measuring those relationships reveals whether the graph grows denser, fragments, or becomes more organized over time. By capturing both the raw data-level facts (which entities link to which) and the schema-level structure (what types of relationships are allowed), you gain a complete picture of how the graph's architecture changes. This enables anyone storing data in graph form to detect quality problems, spot when the graph stops making semantic sense, or understand whether their knowledge base is becoming more or less usable—problems that matter for every system built on structured knowledge.

Wiseswap solves the problem of sharing memory across multiple cloud applications without them interfering with each other. The insight is that when memory requests compete with network traffic, the system can prioritize urgent ones using low-level hardware commands to pause and resume data flows, while simultaneously choosing uncongested paths through the network. The reason this works is that interference is caused by predictable bottlenecks: certain network paths get saturated during peak load, and certain operations (like serving user requests) are more time-critical than background memory transfers. By measuring latency to detect congestion and using priority signals to protect critical traffic, you can reduce wasted effort and idle waiting. This lets cloud providers pack more applications onto shared infrastructure without users noticing slowdowns, improving both utilization and responsiveness.

Glasses adapts a pre-trained vision model to a new environment using just one unlabeled photo from that environment, aided by a cloud server. The method works because a new deployment environment (different lighting, camera angle, or object orientation) creates a shift in what the model sees, but adapting the model's internal feature extractors requires only understanding how the environment looks—not a full training dataset. The cloud computes how to adjust the model based on comparing the environment photo to training data, then sends minimal updates back to the device. This is sound because the model already learned general visual concepts during initial training; retuning those features for the specific environment reuses that knowledge. This solves the real problem: edge devices can't retrain models locally due to limited compute and data, but they must adapt quickly or their accuracy collapses on deployment.

This is a perspective piece on how deep learning and language models are reshaping how web platforms (search, recommendation, conversation) work. No specific mathematical principle is presented, but the underlying insight is that end-to-end learned systems can capture subtle patterns in user intent and content relevance that hand-crafted rules cannot. Deep models succeed because they can compose simple learned features into arbitrarily complex decision boundaries; when trained on massive interaction logs, they automatically discover which combinations of signals predict what users want. This enables systems to move from static ranking to adaptive, interactive experiences that improve as users explore.

BEACOF models social collaboration among agents as a game where each agent maintains beliefs about others' capabilities and must decide whether to cooperate or compete. The method works because in real human groups, people dynamically adjust collaboration strategy based on ongoing evidence about who knows what—a game-theoretic equilibrium where each person's choice, given their beliefs, is the best response to what others are doing. The principle is that when everyone uses sequential reasoning (updating beliefs after each exchange and choosing rationally), the group converges toward stable, high-quality solutions rather than deadlock or false consensus. By formalizing this equilibrium concept, the system prevents agents from getting stuck in unproductive patterns and instead achieves collaborative breakthroughs—making simulations of policy debates, medical decisions, or social dynamics far more realistic.

DMAP solves document understanding by preserving the logical structure humans use when reading: sections nested hierarchically, figures placed near their explanations, cross-references linking concepts. Most systems flatten documents into independent chunks, losing this structure; DMAP instead builds an explicit map showing how text, figures, and tables connect. This works because humans navigate documents via structure—we know that an answer often lives near a figure caption or in the subsection we're reading—and reasoning grounded in that structure is more reliable than searching flat chunks. By capturing both semantic content and spatial position, the system makes retrieval more precise (fewer irrelevant snippets pulled in) and reasoning more coherent (the agent understands context). This addresses the real problem: multimodal documents contain answers that depend on knowing where information is located, not just what it says.

BanditLP combines learning which recommendations work (via neural Thompson Sampling, which explores uncertain options and exploits winners) with a large-scale optimization that applies business constraints (budget limits, fairness rules, inventory) at serving time. The method works because exploration and exploitation must balance—pure exploration wastes time testing bad options, pure exploitation misses better ones—and Thompson Sampling provably converges to the best option under uncertainty. Once you know the likely quality of each recommendation, an optimization solver ensures you pick the best one that also satisfies all constraints. This is sound because the learning and constraint-solving problems are separate: learn what works, then efficiently pick the best feasible choice. At LinkedIn scale, this lets the system simultaneously adapt email strategy to user response while respecting business rules, delivering better engagement without violating policy.

This is a keynote arguing that AI should build persistent models of both physical reality (time, space, cause-and-effect) and human psychology (goals, beliefs, emotions, social norms). The underlying principle is that reasoning about real-world consequences requires knowing not just what happens mechanically, but why it matters to people and what people intend. Systems that maintain such dual models can predict outcomes humans care about and explain their reasoning in human terms. This approach is sound because human decision-making always balances physical outcomes against mental states—we act based on what we believe will happen and how we want to feel. AI that mirrors this reasoning can collaborate with humans rather than surprise or frustrate them, making alignment and trust natural rather than bolted-on.

Time-TK improves time series forecasting by preserving correlations across multiple time steps instead of treating each step as independent. The method works because real-world time series often repeat patterns at specific intervals (hourly patterns in web traffic, weekly patterns in social media), and treating each time step separately destroys that information. The paper shows an upper bound proving that independent embeddings lose information unavoidably, then proposes capturing multi-offset correlations by learning how different time steps relate to each other. This principle applies because web data is highly structured with predictable rhythms; capturing those rhythms makes prediction far more accurate. Forecasting matters for cloud operations, transport systems, and resource planning, where small improvements in accuracy translate directly to cost savings and stability.

SuperG recommends new items by first finding users with similar taste profiles, then mining which of their past behaviors are genuinely informative rather than noise. The method works because new items have no interaction history, so the system must borrow evidence from similar users; the insight is that not all past interactions are equally useful—a user who often clicks videos probably won't prefer text articles, so using their text clicks as evidence is misleading. By identifying truly similar users (via preference signals) and filtering their behavior to extract only actions consistent with their profile, the system reduces spurious neighbors and captures the most reliable learning signal. This applies to new-item problems because similar users' filtering tells you which behaviors actually reflect stable taste. Recommendation platforms face constant new-item streams, so accurate cold-start suggestions directly impact user engagement and discovery.

DHHGN predicts future events in knowledge graphs by capturing both local patterns (how entities near the target interact) and global patterns (which past facts matter most). The method works using two insights: first, high-order interactions among entities matter, not just pairwise links—for example, a person might attend a conference only if specific colleagues also attend, a pattern that requires looking at three-way relationships. Second, not all historical facts equally inform a prediction; a major fact from last year matters more than a routine fact from yesterday. By using a combined structure that captures both many-way entity interactions and adaptive attention to global history, the system models how knowledge graph evolution unfolds. This principle applies because real events depend on multiple prior conditions and on recognizing which past events are relevant—the system learns to separate signal from noise. Forecasting knowledge graph events helps maintain consistency in linked data and anticipates schema updates.

E2SGNN achieves both expressiveness and computational efficiency in graph processing by using spiking neurons (which mimic the brain's efficient binary signals) but modulating them with learned real-valued adjustments at different scales. The method works because binary spiking alone lacks expressive power—it cannot distinguish fine differences—but adding massive real computation defeats the efficiency goal. The solution is to modulate spiking signals globally and locally: global modulation captures large-scale graph structure, local modulation captures fine-grained neighbor relationships, both at minimal cost. This principle applies because graph learning requires discrimination at multiple scales; a good representation captures both community-level and individual-level patterns. By dynamically adjusting how many spike steps each graph needs based on complexity, the system avoids wasting time on simple inputs. This matters for large-scale graph analysis where energy and latency matter, such as social networks and knowledge bases.

This paper studies how inverse propensity scoring (IPS), a classical method for comparing policies in recommendation systems, behaves in practice. IPS is theoretically sound: if you weight observed user interactions by the inverse probability they were shown, the resulting estimate is unbiased—it equals what the policy would achieve on average. The method works under the assumption that whether a user sees an item is independent of that item's quality, an assumption that holds in controlled experiments but often breaks in real logs. The paper shows empirically that even simple synthetic experiments can produce unreliable rankings of different estimators, and that real datasets violate standard assumptions. This matters because practitioners often trust IPS without checking assumptions, leading to misleading policy comparisons and poor recommendation choices. Understanding when and why IPS fails is crucial for trustworthy evaluation.

PRISM decomposes multimodal information into three components—unique (only in one modality), redundant (repeated across modalities), and synergistic (emerging only from combining modalities)—then weights them per user. The method works because modalities carry different information: an image shows visual style, text describes function, audio conveys emotion. Some information is unique to each modality, some is repeated (text and image both show color), but the most valuable signal often emerges only when modalities are combined (an image and caption together create context neither provides alone). By decomposing and weighting these components adaptively, the system learns which combinations matter for each user—some users care about visual appeal, others about detailed descriptions. This principle applies because users have different preferences, and forcing a fixed modality combination serves nobody optimally. Sequential recommendation at scale requires personalized fusion to maximize relevance.

MinSAR unifies search (where users state intent explicitly via queries) and recommendation (where intent is implicit in past clicks) by learning a shared representation of user interest using quantized dimensions. The method works because both systems predict what users want, but search sees explicit signals (queries) and recommendation sees implicit signals (behavior), and these often contradict—a user queries for a product but clicks competitor reviews. By forcing both signals into a compact shared space using quantization, the system finds coherent interest representations that work across both scenarios. The principle is that true user interest usually underlies both behaviors; by learning it as a latent code rather than keeping signals separate, the system reduces conflicts and knowledge sharing becomes effective. Task-specific experts then apply this unified interest differently (semantic matching for search, collaborative filtering for recommendation), each optimized for its role. This addresses the real problem: single-scenario platforms lose users who move between search and discovery, while unified systems compete across both channels simultaneously.
